sections.html:
Farmington is the Davis County seat, set between Ogden and Salt Lake City with a commute of about a half hour to job centers in both. The 2020 census counted 24,531 people, up from 18,275 in 2010, and most homes are owned by the people living in them. Plenty of owners here carry real equity, yet some still hit an old tax bill, an unpermitted basement apartment or a valuation they dislike before they list.

Below you will find the county tax calendar, the appeal route, the city's accessory unit rules and the steps of a direct cash sale.

sections.h2: Property tax due dates and penalties
sections.html:
Farmington parcels are billed through Davis County, on dates set by the Utah calendar. The bill is due November 30. After that day an unpaid balance is delinquent, but the penalty shrinks if you clear the whole amount by January 31.

The 45% primary residential exemption means the county taxes your main home on only 55% of its market value. A rental or a second house gets no such discount, so an owner who has moved out should expect a heavier bill.

Tax Administration sits at 61 South Main Street, Room 101, and answers at 801-451-3331.

Late in July the Davis County Controller mails each owner a Notice of Assessors' Property Market Valuation. Think the number is too high? Take it to the Board of Equalization, which is the Davis County Commission. Filing closes in mid-September, and a call to 801-451-3331 gets you the exact day.

The rate itself is off the table; the hearing deals with market value only. The owner files, or an agent who holds a notarized authorization. Useful proof includes:

  • closing documents signed by the title agent,
  • a full appraisal by a certified appraiser,
  • sales of at least three comparable properties near January 1,
  • documented factual errors, such as the wrong square footage.

A lower value helps only for as long as you own the house, so weigh the effort against your plans to sell.

Farmington allows two kinds of accessory units and a third route that lets an owner put a detached unit on its own lot. Only one ADU is allowed per single-family home.

  • Internal ADU: inside or attached to the main home, on a lot of at least 6,000 square feet.
  • Detached ADU: a permanent structure on a foundation, on a lot of at least 10,000 square feet.
  • Subordinate single-family dwelling: a separate lot with its own home, subject to subdivision approval.

An owner has to live in either the main home or the ADU. After a subordinate dwelling is split off, the owner must occupy it for two years. Every unit needs a full kitchen, a full bathroom and a parking space off the street on top of the main home's, and tenants must stay 30 days or longer, which rules out nightly rentals.

Turning existing space into an internal ADU takes a building permit unless the space was already approved for living. An unpapered basement unit can hold up a buyer who needs a mortgage, because the lender's appraiser will ask about it.

Winters here are real, and lake-enhanced snow can arrive in the cold months. Flash floods have hit the town in past decades, so a lot close to a creek or canyon mouth deserves a second look. The Farmington Area Pressurized Irrigation District has served homeowners since July 1978, which makes irrigation a common buyer question.

  • Check with your insurer on flood coverage if the parcel is near a creek or canyon mouth.
  • Write down the roof's age and any snow or water repairs.
  • Find out if your yard runs on pressurized irrigation.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work in Farmington?
sections.html:
With no lender involved, there is no appraisal gap and no loan approval to wait on. You describe the house, we compare it with recent sales close by, and the offer is yours to take or leave.

  1. Send us the address and a few details about the house.
  2. We look over the property and the surrounding blocks.
  3. You say yes or no to the offer, with no obligation.
  4. A title company searches the record and picks a closing date with you.
  5. The deed is recorded and the funds reach you at closing.

Closing lands on a day that suits you and the title company, so a move can line up with a new job, a school year or a purchase elsewhere. Nobody tours the house, and no repair list comes back to haggle over.

On closing day you sign at the title company, the deed goes on record, and the proceeds arrive after any mortgage payoff and unpaid tax balance are settled. Ask for the settlement figures ahead of time so the final number holds no surprises. A traditional sale usually spends weeks on showings, inspection requests and loan approval, and a cash sale compresses most of that into the title work alone.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes owed or an unpermitted unit
sections.html:
Owe taxes, or have an ADU that never got its permit? Say so to the title company at the outset. The title search will turn up back taxes anyway, and they are normally paid from the sale proceeds at closing.

Farmington owners who talk to us usually describe one of these:

  • A dated house in or beside the historic district.
  • A basement apartment built without an internal ADU permit.
  • A back unit the owner would like to sell apart from the house, which the city handles as a subordinate single-family dwelling with subdivision approval.
  • A valuation notice the owner disputes and wants to appeal before a sale.

Any of them can drag out a regular listing. Selling directly means no staging, no repairs and a schedule you control.

sections.h2: What to gather before you call
sections.html: A folder of paperwork shortens the road to closing. Gather the latest tax notice, the July valuation notice, permits for additions or a basement unit, and receipts for roof or water repairs. If you rent a unit, have the lease terms handy, since the 30-day minimum applies to ADU rentals here. A recent mortgage statement helps the title company work out the payoff, and a photo of the roof, the furnace and any basement kitchen lets us give you a realistic offer on the first call. If someone else lives in the house, tell us at the start so timing and access are clear to everyone.

faqs.q: What county is Farmington, Utah in?
faqs.a: Davis County. The city is the seat of the county, and Tax Administration is at 61 South Main Street, Room 101.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Farmington?
faqs.a: November 30. After that the balance is delinquent, and paying everything by January 31 reduces the penalty.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Farmington property value?
faqs.a: Send the appeal to the Davis County Board of Equalization once the late-July valuation notice arrives. The deadline is in mid-September, so confirm the date with Tax Administration. Market value is the only thing you can contest.

faqs.q: Can I rent out a Farmington ADU for short stays?
faqs.a: No. Tenants must stay at least 30 days, and an owner has to live in the main home or the ADU.

faqs.q: What size lot do I need for a detached ADU in Farmington?
faqs.a: A detached unit calls for a lot of at least 10,000 square feet, while an internal one needs at least 6,000.
